_meta.descricao: Specific institutes and procedures of Canon Law — matrimonial nullity, excommunication, censures, and others —, at a greater level of detail than the overview of the category Structure of the Church.
_meta.aviso: Introductory presentation of juridical institutes; it does not replace qualified canonical counsel for concrete cases.

itens.resumo: The systematic collection of laws governing the organization and life of the Latin Rite Catholic Church, in force in its current form since 1983.
itens.corpo:
The Code of Canon Law (Codex Iuris Canonici) is the official compilation of the laws that govern the organization, government, and discipline of the Latin Church. Its current form was promulgated by John Paul II on January 25, 1983, by the Apostolic Constitution Sacrae Disciplinae Leges, and entered into force on the First Sunday of Advent of that year, November 27, replacing the 1917 Code in light of the reforms of the Second Vatican Council. The pontiff himself described the new code as "the last document of the Second Vatican Council," emphasizing its continuity with conciliar ecclesiology. Only the Latin text has the force of law.

The history of modern codification begins with Pius X, who, by the motu proprio Arduum sane munus, of March 19, 1904, established the Pontifical Commission for the Codification of Canon Law, presided over by the then Cardinal Pietro Gasparri. The first Code — also called the Pio-Benedictine Code — was promulgated by Benedict XV on May 27, 1917, and entered into force on May 19, 1918. Then, on January 25, 1959, John XXIII announced, together with the convocation of the Second Vatican Council, the intention to reform the 1917 Code; the revision commission (Pontificia Commissio Codici Iuris Canonici Recognoscendo), established in 1963, worked during the pontificates of Paul VI and John Paul II until the work was completed.

The 1983 Code is organized into seven "books": I. General Norms; II. The People of God; III. The Teaching Function of the Church; IV. The Sanctifying Function of the Church; V. The Temporal Goods of the Church; VI. Sanctions in the Church; VII. Processes. It is composed of 1752 canons (compared with 2414 in the 1917 Code), and in its canon 1 it declares that the canons refer only to the Latin Church. The Eastern Catholic Churches have their own code, the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990).

The text is not immutable: it has been updated by later pontifical acts, such as the motu proprio Ad Tuendam Fidem (1998) and, more recently, the Apostolic Constitution Praedicate Evangelium, of March 19, 2022, on the Roman Curia, in force since June 5, 2022, which amended provisions of Book II concerning the organization of the Curia, suppressing pontifical congregations and councils in favor of dicasteries. It nonetheless remains the fundamental legal corpus of the Latin Church, a landmark of contemporary canonical discipline.

itens.resumo: The ecclesiastical declaration that a marriage, because it lacked some essential element from the beginning, was never valid — made by a competent tribunal and not to be confused with civil divorce.
itens.corpo:
The declaration of matrimonial nullity is not a "Catholic divorce," as it is popularly mistaken to be, but the recognition, by an ecclesiastical tribunal, that a given marriage never validly existed from its beginning, because it lacked some essential element required by Canon Law. The 1983 Code lists the typical causes in three groups: defects of consent (canons 1095-1103 — lack of capacity to assume the essential obligations of marriage due to causes of a psychic nature, ignorance, error, simulation, force or grave fear, a condition not fulfilled); diriment impediments (canons 1083-1094 — age, impotence, a prior bond not dissolved, disparity of worship, sacred orders, perpetual religious profession, abduction, crime, consanguinity, affinity, public propriety, and legal kinship arising from adoption); and the lack of canonical form in the celebration (canons 1108-1123). The Code lists, altogether, about nineteen titles of nullity frequently invoked in practice.

Among all of them, canon 1095 — which deals with incapacity to consent — is the one most often invoked in contemporary cases, because it touches the delicate boundary between affective maturity and immaturity. In not a few cases, tribunals turn to the assistance of experts in psychology, which has given rise to debates about the extent to which the norm has been interpreted. The central juridical principle is that matrimonial consent (canon 1057) is the element that constitutes the bond: if it was lacking in some essential respect at the moment of the celebration, there is no marriage, and the Church merely declares it.

The procedure has been the object of growing attention. On January 25, 2005, the Pontifical Council for Legislative Texts published, with the approval of John Paul II, the Instruction "Dignitas Connubii," gathering into a single document the norms to be observed in diocesan and interdiocesan tribunals in matrimonial cases. Ten years later, Pope Francis promulgated, on August 15, 2015, the motu proprio "Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus" (in force from December 8 of the same year, the solemnity of the Immaculate Conception and the fiftieth anniversary of the close of the Second Vatican Council), which reformed and streamlined the process. The reform introduced the possibility of a "briefer process" before the diocesan Bishop himself in cases where nullity is supported by particularly evident arguments, making the procedure more accessible, swifter and less costly. Francis reaffirmed, however, that the change affects only the process — its instrumentality — and not the doctrine of the indissolubility of marriage. A complementary motu proprio, "Mitis et misericors Iesus," extended an analogous reform to the Eastern Catholic Churches.

itens.resumo: The gravest canonical censure, which excludes a baptized person from certain acts of sacramental life and from ecclesiastical offices until he is reconciled, having a medicinal rather than a definitively condemnatory character.
itens.corpo:
Excommunication is the most severe censure (medicinal penalty) in Canon Law, provided for in canons 1331 ff. of the 1983 Code of Canon Law. It does not revoke baptism nor expel the faithful from the Church: the excommunicated person remains a Christian, but is forbidden to have any ministerial participation in the celebration of the Sacrifice of the Eucharist or in any other ceremonies of worship, to celebrate the sacraments or to receive them, and to exercise ecclesiastical offices, ministries, or functions of governance in the Church (can. 1331 §1). For the penalty to be removed, the offender must cease from contumacy — the obstinate persistence in the offense —, repent, and seek absolution from the competent authority; can. 1358 §1 establishes that remission cannot be denied to one who has withdrawn from contumacy.

The penalty can be latae sententiae (automatic, incurred by the very commission of the offense) or ferendae sententiae (which only takes effect when imposed by the authority). The 1917 Code defined this distinction, and can. 1318 of the current Code establishes that the legislator is not to threaten censures — especially excommunication — except with great moderation and only for the more serious and malicious offenses. Among the offenses that carry excommunication latae sententiae are apostasy, heresy, and schism (can. 1364 §1); procured and completed abortion (can. 1398); the desecration of the consecrated species, by throwing them away or taking or retaining them for a sacrilegious purpose (can. 1367); physical force against the Roman Pontiff, without excluding dismissal from the clerical state if the offender is a cleric (can. 1370 §1); the consecration of a bishop without a pontifical mandate, as well as the one who receives the consecration from him (can. 1382); the direct violation of the sacramental seal (can. 1388 §1); and the absolution of an accomplice in a sin against the sixth commandment (can. 1378). Several of these cases are reserved to the Apostolic See, that is, absolution depends on Rome. In danger of death, however, any priest can absolve from all censures (can. 976), and the confessor can remit non-reserved and undeclared censures when it is hard for the penitent to remain in a state of grave sin (can. 1357 §1).

Historically, the discipline recognized the distinction between excommunicates who were vitandi ("to be avoided") and tolerati ("tolerated"), introduced by Pope Martin V in the constitution Ad evitanda scandala (1418), at the Council of Constance, in reaction to the abusive and coercive use of excommunication in the Middle Ages. Only one who had been publicly declared such by name, or who had physically attacked the Pope, was vitandus; the others were tolerated. This category, still present in the constitution Apostolicae Sedis of Pius IX (1869) and in the 1917 Code, fell into oblivion with the 1983 Code, which unified the figure of excommunication and emphasized its medicinal character.

One of the most famous episodes in the history of excommunication was the break with Martin Luther. After the bull Exsurge Domine (1520), which threatened the German friar with excommunication if he did not retract the forty-one censured theses, Luther publicly burned the copy of the bull on December 10, 1520, at the Elster Gate in Wittenberg. In response, Pope Leo X published the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, of January 3, 1521, which excommunicated Luther and some of his supporters, among them Andreas Karlstadt. The text decreed against them the sentences of excommunication, anathema, and interdict, as well as the deprivation of dignities and goods and the confiscation of their possessions. At the end of the twentieth century, in dialogue with the Catholic Church, Lutherans asked for the lifting of Luther's excommunication; the response of the Roman Curia was that the custom is to lift excommunication only from persons who are still living.

itens.resumo: The "medicinal" penalties of Canon Law — excommunication, interdict and suspension — which seek the conversion of the faithful before punishing them, regulated in canons 1331-1335 of the 1983 Code.
itens.corpo:
Censures (or "medicinal" penalties) are one of the two great types of penalty in Canon Law, alongside expiatory penalties: canon 1312 §1 presents them as the "poenae medicinales seu censurae" listed in canons 1331-1333. They comprise three degrees: excommunication (the most serious, which deprives one of participation in the sacraments and forbids the offender any ministerial participation in the celebration of the Eucharist or of other ceremonies of worship, according to canon 1331 §1), interdict (which subjects the guilty party to the same liturgical prohibitions, but without excluding him from ecclesial communion in the full sense, canon 1332) and suspension (applicable only to clerics, which restricts acts of the power of orders, of the power of governance, and the exercise of rights or functions of an office, canon 1333).

Their declared purpose is not punitive in the strict sense, but medicinal: they seek to bring about repentance and amendment in the faithful, ceasing as soon as the person reforms and is validly absolved or dispensed. The Code itself distinguishes, in canon 1314, between "ferendae sententiae" penalties (which bind the guilty party only after they have been imposed by a sentence) and "latae sententiae" penalties (which are incurred automatically by violation of the law, without the need for judicial application). The canonical tradition links excommunication to exclusion from ecclesial communion: the corresponding word, "anathema", designated the offender separated from the body of the Church, and classical doctrine has always insisted on its corrective rather than merely vindictive character.

The penal regime of the Latin Church received decisive systematization in the Decretum Gratiani (the Concordia discordantium canonum, of the twelfth century, attributed to the monk and jurist Gratian), which gathered and harmonized the discipline that was then scattered. The 1917 Code and, later, the 1983 Code (reorganized in canons 1311-1399, distributed in Book VI — Sanctions in the Church) gave precise juridical form to the censures. Historical examples of latae sententiae excommunication reserved to the Holy See include cases such as those of canons 1370 (§1, physical violence against the Roman Pontiff), 1382 (§1, desecration of the Eucharistic species) and 1398 (§2, procured abortion), among others.

In 2021, Pope Francis published the Apostolic Constitution "Pascite Gregem Dei" (June 1, in force on December 8), which entirely reformed Book VI — the greatest revision of canonical penal law since 1983. Preceded by a long process of consultation begun in the pontificate of Benedict XVI, the reform added or aggravated offenses (violation of pontifical secrecy, illegitimate abandonment of ministry, child pornography, failure to report, abuse of authority) and reaffirmed the principle of proportionality in the application of penalties, balancing the three purposes attributed to every sanction: the conversion of the offender, the reparation of the harm and the prevention of scandal. The reform also stressed that there is no pastoral charity without correction — as Francis himself sums it up, there is no "mercy" detached from the justice that heals.

itens.resumo: The canonical distinction between the intimate sphere of conscience, dealt with in confession and spiritual direction, and the public and juridical sphere of the Church.
itens.corpo:
Canon Law distinguishes the "internal forum" — the sphere of personal conscience — from the "external forum," the public and institutional sphere in which the Church exercises her visible juridical authority, by means of trials, sanctions and administrative acts. The distinction goes back to Roman law (the forum internum as the forum of conscience) and was incorporated into the canonical tradition especially from the Middle Ages onward, when penitential discipline became established with the constitution Omnis utriusque sexus of the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), which imposed annual confession to one's own pastor.

The internal forum is in turn subdivided into two distinct spheres. The "internal sacramental forum" is that of Confession: in it the priest forgives sins in the name of God, and everything he hears is protected by the sacramental seal, which the 1983 Code of Canon Law declares "inviolable" (can. 983 §1), and which cannot be broken even by the penitent himself. The "internal extra-sacramental forum" — hidden, but external to the sacrament of Penance — encompasses spiritual direction and other ministries of counsel, in which the Church grants graces, dissolves juridical bonds such as censures and attends to the sanctification of souls, without however forgiving sins. The Note of the Apostolic Penitentiary on the Importance of the Internal Forum and the Inviolability of the Sacramental Seal, of June 29, 2019, is the most explicit recent document on this threefold distinction and on the proper identity of the extra-sacramental forum.

In the external forum the Church acts publicly: she establishes and governs tribunals, imposes penalties, grants dispensations, judges the validity of marriage and administers worship. A sin or an irregularity may have been resolved in the internal forum through confession without producing any juridical effect in the external forum, and vice versa: no one can be condemned in the external forum on the basis of matter exclusively confessed, since the seal is an absolute obstacle to proof. A good attainable in the external forum (such as the dispensation from a matrimonial impediment) is not obtained by mere sacramental absolution, and the remission of a censure in the internal forum does not by itself undo the public effects of the censure.

The direct violation of the sacramental seal by the confessor is a most grave delict: the Code of 1983, in the wording confirmed by the penal reform of the apostolic constitution Pascite gregem Dei (2021), imposes on a confessor who violates it excommunication latae sententiae reserved to the Apostolic See, and punishes with a just penalty one who does so only indirectly. This distinction of forums protects, at one and the same time, the inviolable freedom of conscience before God and the public juridical order necessary for the governance of the Church.

itens.titulo: The Canonization Process as a Juridical Institution
itens.resumo: The causes of saints follow a rigorous canonical procedure, with diocesan and Roman phases governed by a special pontifical law (can. 1403) and by the constitution "Divinus Perfectionis Magister" (1983).
itens.corpo:
Although holiness is a spiritual reality, its official recognition by the Church takes on a juridical form. The 1983 Code of Canon Law does not directly regulate the rite, but refers to it: canon 1403 provides that "the causes of canonization of the Servants of God are governed by special pontifical law," with the norms of the Code itself applying subsidiarily when the special law refers to universal law. This "special law" found its most recent form in the apostolic constitution "Divinus Perfectionis Magister," promulgated by John Paul II on January 25, 1983, accompanied by the "Normae Servandae in inquisitionibus ab Episcopis faciendis in causis sanctorum." The text was drawn up after the creation, by Paul VI in 1969 (constitution "Sacra Rituum Congregatio"), of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, separated from the former Congregation of Rites — today a Dicastery, whose competence is recognized by the constitution "Praedicate Evangelium."

The procedure is divided into two major phases. The first is diocesan: it is the responsibility of the bishop of the place where the candidate died — either on his own initiative, or at the request of the faithful, of associations, or of their representatives — to investigate the life, the virtues, the martyrdom, the reputation for holiness, and any miracles. Only after five years have passed since the death may the petition (libellus) be presented by a postulator (a requirement the Pope may dispense); the "Normae Servandae" (nos. 7-9) further distinguish "recent" causes, proved by eyewitnesses, from "ancient" ones, which depend on written sources, requiring special caution when the request is presented more than thirty years after the death, in order to rule out fraud or undue delay. Before the bishop establishes the tribunal, the Holy See must grant the "Nihil obstat" decree — that is, that nothing stands in the way of the cause. Testimonies are gathered, the candidate's writings are examined, and the process is closed, with its acts sent to Rome.

The second phase is Roman. A relator is appointed who guides the postulator in preparing the "Positio" — the volume that synthesizes the evidence in order to reconstruct the life and demonstrate the heroic virtues, the martyrdom or the offering of life, in addition to the reputation for holiness. The "Positio," which should not exceed about 500 pages, is submitted to the examination of a commission of theologians (and, in ancient causes, also of historians); if the opinion is favorable, the cardinals and bishops of the Dicastery give their judgment, and it is for the Pope to promulgate the decree of heroic virtues. From then on the Servant of God is called Venerable. The miracle is the object of a distinct process, examined with the help of a medical commission composed of believing and non-believing specialists, which assesses whether the cure is complete, lasting, and scientifically inexplicable.

The institution underwent a profound reform in 1983, regarded as the most radical since the decrees of Urban VIII in the seventeenth century. The office of the Promoter of the Faith — the "advocatus diaboli" or "devil's advocate" — was, in practice, suppressed; it had been created by Sixtus V in 1587, and its function was to argue against canonization, point out flaws of character and inconsistencies in the evidence, and test the reputation for holiness; its role of contradiction, with veto power, was replaced by the College of Relators and by a moderator secretary, with the declared aim of making the process simpler, faster, and less costly. Critics point out that the reform eliminated safeguards previously maintained by popes such as Alexander III, Sixtus V, and Benedict XIV; figures are often cited in this debate: John Paul II canonized 482 people and beatified 1,338 between 1978 and 2005, compared with about 300 canonizations in the period from 1587 to 1983.

For beatification, the ordinary path of heroic virtues requires the recognition of a miracle attributed to the intercession of the Venerable; a candidate declared a martyr becomes Blessed immediately, with the miracle dispensed. For canonization, a new miracle occurring after beatification is required as a rule — although a particularity is acknowledged: the beatified martyr generally needs a miracle to be canonized, and there is the instrument of the pontifical dispensation "ad cautelam" regarding the time of the miracle. Since 2017, Francis's motu proprio "Maiorem hac dilectionem" has added the path of the "offering of life," distinct from both martyrdom and the heroicity of virtues and which, like the latter, requires a miracle for beatification. Canonization, an act reserved to the Roman Pontiff, is definitive and irreformable, and only the servants of God thus inscribed by the authority of the Church may receive public veneration (can. 1187).

itens.titulo: Rights and Duties of the Faithful
itens.resumo: The 1983 Code of Canon Law (canons 208-223) recognizes in all the baptized a true statute of fundamental rights in the Church, together with corresponding duties.
itens.corpo:
The 1983 Code of Canon Law, reflecting the ecclesiology of communion of the Second Vatican Council (notably the dogmatic Constitution "Lumen Gentium"), devotes Title I of Book II — "The Obligations and Rights of All the Christian Faithful" — a set of sixteen canons (208 to 223) that constitutes what may be called the fundamental statute of the Christian faithful. The starting point is found in canon 96: "By baptism one is incorporated into the Church of Christ and is constituted a person in it with the duties and rights which are proper to Christians". It is from baptism, and not from office or sacred orders, that ecclesial personality and the juridical capacity to act in the Church arise.

This section of the Code recognizes the fundamental equality among all the faithful. Canon 208 declares that, "from their rebirth in Christ, there exists among all the Christian faithful a true equality regarding dignity and action", by which all cooperate in the building up of the Body of Christ according to each one's own condition and function. On this basis, it enumerates concrete rights and duties: always to maintain communion with the Church (canon 209); to strive to lead a holy life and to promote the growth of the Church (canon 210); to work so that the message of salvation may reach all (canon 211); to accept with Christian obedience what the pastors teach and, at the same time, to have the freedom to make known to them their needs and desires and, according to their own competence, the right — and at times even the duty — to manifest their opinion on matters which pertain to the good of the Church (canon 212); to receive from the pastors spiritual goods, especially the word of God and the sacraments (canon 213); to live their own spirituality and their own approved rite (canon 214); to found and direct freely associations for purposes of charity, piety, and apostolate (canon 215); to promote and sustain apostolic action, without claiming the name "Catholic" without the consent of the authority (canon 216); to receive a Christian education (canon 217).

The Code also protects more personal dimensions: the right to freedom of inquiry and to express one's opinion in matters of one's own competence, with due submission to the magisterium (canon 218); immunity from any coercion in choosing a state of life (canon 219); the right to a good reputation and to privacy, which no one may unlawfully harm (canon 220); and the right to vindicate and defend legitimately one's own rights in the competent ecclesiastical forum, to be judged according to the prescripts of the law applied with equity, and not to be punished with canonical penalties except in accord with the law (canon 221). Corresponding to these rights are the duties to assist with the needs of the Church and to promote social justice (canon 222), always with the restraint that prevents rights from being exercised to the detriment of the common good and of the discipline of the Church (canon 223).

This is a relatively recent juridical development. In classical canon law, the laity were treated above all as subjects, and not as holders of rights of their own founded on baptism. Only with the ecclesiology of Vatican II — which restored to the laity their condition as active members of the People of God — was the legislator able to recognize formally in the ordinary member of the faithful a dignity and a participation previously less explicit. It is no coincidence that canon 212 §§2-3 (the right to make known needs and opinions to the pastors) is today regarded as one of the most significant for ecclesial life, since it provides a juridical basis for the co-responsibility and synodality of all the baptized.

itens.resumo: The circumstances established by law that render a person incapable of validly contracting marriage — diriment impediments — unless dispensed by the competent authority.
itens.corpo:
Marriage impediments are circumstances established by Canon Law that render a person incapable of validly contracting marriage until they are removed or dispensed. The 1983 Code of Canon Law treats diriment impediments in general in canons 1073 to 1082 and, in particular, in Chapter III (canons 1083 to 1094), which lists twelve figures: age, impotence, prior bond, disparity of worship, sacred orders, perpetual religious profession, abduction, crime (conjugicide), consanguinity, affinity, public propriety, and legal relationship arising from adoption.

Can. 1083 sets the minimum age for validity at sixteen completed years for the man and fourteen for the woman, and episcopal conferences may require a higher age for liceity (in Brazil, eighteen and sixteen years). Can. 1084 declares antecedent and perpetual impotence to perform the conjugal act, whether absolute or relative, to be diriment — but sterility neither nullifies nor prohibits marriage. Can. 1085 establishes as an impediment the bond of a prior marriage validly contracted, even if not consummated: this is the so-called ligamen (prior bond), which is of divine law and therefore cannot be overcome by any ecclesiastical authority. Also included are disparity of worship (marriage with an unbaptized person, can. 1086), sacred orders (diaconate, presbyterate or episcopate, can. 1087), a public perpetual vow of chastity in a religious institute (can. 1088), abduction (can. 1089), and crime or conjugicide — one who attempts the life of a spouse in order to marry another (can. 1090).

The impediment of consanguinity (can. 1091) invalidates marriage in the direct line between all ascendants and descendants, and in the collateral line up to the fourth degree inclusive; the impediment is not multiplied, and marriage is never permitted as long as a doubt remains about consanguinity in the direct line or in the second degree of the collateral line. Affinity in the direct line is diriment in any degree (can. 1092). Public propriety arises from an invalid marriage after common life has been established or from notorious concubinage, and it invalidates marriage in the first degree of the direct line (can. 1093). Legal relationship arising from adoption prevents marriage between the adopter and the adoptee and between the adoptee and the closest relatives of the other (can. 1094).

Doctrine distinguishes impediments of divine law — which cannot be overcome by any ecclesiastical authority, such as the bond of a prior valid marriage, sacred orders as regards the presbyterate, and the closest degrees of consanguinity — from those of merely ecclesiastical law, which the competent authority can dispense for a just cause. Dispensation is reserved to the Holy See in cases of sacred orders, of a public perpetual vow of chastity in an institute of pontifical right, and of the impediment of crime; a dispensation from consanguinity in the direct line or in the second degree of the collateral line is never granted. In danger of death, however, the local Ordinary can dispense from all impediments of ecclesiastical law, except the one arising from the order of the presbyterate (can. 1079 §1).

Historically, impediments of kinship were treated from the Decretum Gratiani (12th century) onward by means of "trees" or tables of consanguinity and affinity, which illustrated the prohibited degrees — hence the medieval miniatures that represent these degrees as family trees. The matter took its present form in the 1917 codification and was retained, with adjustments, in the 1983 Code.

itens.resumo: The right of every member of the faithful to appeal, by judicial or administrative means, against decisions of ecclesiastical authority, whether administrative or judicial, that he or she considers unjust.
itens.corpo:
Canon Law provides formal mechanisms for challenging decisions that a member of the faithful considers unjust, distinguishing two main avenues. The first is the judicial avenue: the appeal of sentences of ecclesiastical tribunals to higher instances. The 1983 Code governs it beginning with can. 1628, which recognizes the right of anyone who feels aggrieved by a sentence to appeal to the higher tribunal; the appeal must be lodged within peremptory time limits counted from the official notification of the sentence (can. 1630), and the case moves up through the levels as far as the Roman Rota, the ordinary appellate tribunal of the Holy See. The same case may go through first and second instance and, if necessary, a third, ensuring that no decision becomes definitive without collegial review.

The second avenue is administrative: hierarchical recourse against administrative decrees, regulated by canons 1732 to 1739. Before having recourse, the interested party must ask the author of the decree to revoke or amend it; if he receives no reply within ten working days, or if the reply is unfavorable, he may submit the recourse to the competent hierarchical superior within the peremptory time limit of fifteen working days (can. 1734 and 1737 §2). Once lodged, the recourse does not necessarily suspend the execution of the decree, unless otherwise provided (can. 1736). The author of the decree has thirty days to decide on the petition (can. 1735), and the superior's decision ends the legal conflict, whether definitively or provisionally.

At the head of the administrative jurisdiction is the Supreme Tribunal of the Apostolic Signatura. As the administrative tribunal of the Roman Curia, it is competent to judge recourses against singular administrative acts issued by dicasteries of the Curia or approved by them, to resolve conflicts of competence between tribunals that do not depend on the same appellate tribunal, and to exercise vigilance over the correct administration of justice. It is divided into two functional sections, that of grace and that of justice, inheriting the former distinction between the Signatura gratiae and the Signatura iustitiae.

This entire procedural edifice rests on a theological and juridical principle: ecclesiastical authority too is subject to law and may not act arbitrarily. The faithful are not mere objects of administration but subjects of legitimate rights, in the order of salvation and of communion, for the defense of which the legal order places concrete instruments at their disposal, whether before the tribunals, or before hierarchical superiors and the dicasteries of the Holy See. In exceptional cases, the avenue of recourse may reach the Roman Pontiff himself, supreme legislator, judge and pastor of the Church.
fontes: Code of Canon Law (1983), canons 1628, 1630, 1732-1739
Profile of the Supreme Tribunal of the Apostolic Signatura (official website of the Holy See)

itens.resumo: An act by which the competent executive authority releases a member of the faithful, in a concrete case, from the observance of a merely ecclesiastical law, requiring a just and proportionate cause.
itens.corpo:
Dispensation is defined by the Code of Canon Law itself as "the relaxation of a merely ecclesiastical law in a particular case" (can. 85). It is an institute of Book I (General Norms), in the title dedicated to singular administrative acts, alongside decrees, precepts, rescripts and privileges. By its nature, dispensation applies only to merely ecclesiastical law — that is, to laws that the Church has established by her own authority —, never to divine law, whether natural or positive, whose essential precepts the Church cannot relax. Can. 86 makes this barrier explicit: laws are not subject to dispensation to the extent that they define those things which are essentially constitutive of juridic institutes or acts.

The competence to dispense belongs to those who have executive power over the law in question, within the limits of their jurisdiction, and also to those to whom the law or a legitimate delegation grants this faculty. The diocesan Bishop can dispense the faithful from disciplinary laws, whether universal or particular, issued by the supreme authority of the Church for his territory or his subjects, whenever he judges that it contributes to their spiritual good, but not from procedural or penal laws, nor from those whose dispensation the Apostolic See has reserved to itself (can. 87). The local Ordinary can dispense from diocesan laws and, whenever he judges that it contributes to the good of the faithful, from laws issued by the plenary or provincial Council or by the Conference of Bishops (can. 88). The pastor and other presbyters or deacons, on the other hand, cannot dispense from universal or particular law, unless this power has been expressly granted to them (can. 89).

The distinctive doctrine of the institute is the requirement of a cause: "A dispensation from an ecclesiastical law is not to be granted without a just and reasonable cause, taking into account the circumstances of the case and the gravity of the law from which dispensation is given; otherwise the dispensation is illicit and, unless it is given by the legislator himself or his superior, also invalid" (can. 90 §1). In case of doubt about the sufficiency of the cause, the dispensation is granted validly and licitly (can. 90 §2), since the law presumes good faith. One who possesses the power of dispensing can exercise it even outside his territory, in favor of his subjects who are absent and, unless the contrary is expressly stated, of travelers who are present in his territory (can. 91). The faculty of dispensing granted for a determined case must be interpreted strictly (can. 92), and a dispensation with successive effect ceases in the same way as a privilege ceases, as well as by the total cessation of the cause that motivated it (can. 93).

In practice, dispensation is widely used in matrimonial matters: in impediments of consanguinity and affinity in degrees not reserved to the Pope, in the lack of canonical age, in the canonical form of marriage, and in the so-called lesser impediments, always on the basis of a proven just cause. It also applies to the observance of days of feast and penance (can. 1245), to the minimum age for ordination, and to irregularities. A frequently misunderstood point is the dissolution of the marriage bond: when there is a ratified and consummated marriage — which "cannot be dissolved by any human power or by any cause other than death" (can. 1141) —, the Roman Pontiff can, for a just cause, dissolve a non-consummated marriage (can. 1142), and a natural marriage between non-baptized persons is also dissolved in favor of the faith by the so-called Pauline privilege (canons 1143-1147), as well as in cases of the Petrine privilege (canons 1148-1149). Such cases, however, are not properly "dispensation", but the exercise of a different power, which clearly illustrates the insurmountable limit of the institute: nothing that belongs to the divine constitution of the Church can be the object of relaxation.
fontes: Code of Canon Law (1983), canons 85-93, 1245, 1141-1149

itens.resumo: The period between the death or resignation of a pope (or bishop) and the election of his successor, governed by specific norms that suspend certain acts of governance.
itens.corpo: "Sede vacante" designates the period in which an episcopal see — most notably the See of Rome — is without a titular, whether by death or by resignation, as occurred with Benedict XVI in 2013. In the case of the papacy, this period is governed by specific norms (currently the constitution «Universi Dominici Gregis», of 1996): the day-to-day governance of the Church passes to the College of Cardinals, but with limited powers — they may not innovate in doctrinal or disciplinary matters, these decisions being reserved to the newly elected pope. The same principle, on a diocesan scale, applies to the vacancy of an ordinary episcopal see, administered by a vicar capitular or diocesan administrator until the appointment of a new bishop.

fontes: John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution «Universi Dominici Gregis» (1996)

itens.resumo: An international treaty between the Holy See and a sovereign State, regulating matters of common interest between the Church and the civil power.
itens.corpo:
A concordat is a bilateral treaty concluded between the Holy See — a subject of international law, which represents the Catholic Church on the external plane — and a sovereign State. It is distinguished from other instruments such as "agreements" and the "modus vivendi," which usually deal with more limited matters; in general, a concordat regulates the whole of the juridical status of the Church in the contracting country, recognizing its juridical personality, its freedom of worship and of organization, and governing religious marriage with civil effects, religious education, spiritual assistance (including military and hospital chaplaincy), the appointment of bishops, and the tax regime of ecclesiastical property.

The genre has medieval roots: the Concordat of Worms — also called the Pactum Calixtinum —, signed on September 23, 1122 between Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V of the Holy Roman Empire, ended the Investiture Controversy. By this settlement, the emperor recognized the Church's right to invest bishops and abbots with the ring and the crosier, symbols of spiritual authority, and guaranteed free canonical election and consecration; Callixtus II, for his part, granted Henry the privilege that elections in German dioceses and abbeys be held in his presence, with the emperor being entitled to decide in favor of the "sounder part" in case of a division of the electoral body, and that the one elected receive from him the temporal regalia. The compromise, negotiated over weeks in Mainz and Worms, was one of the first documents to fix in writing the boundary between spiritual and temporal power.

In the modern era, the Concordat of 1801 between Napoleon Bonaparte, then First Consul, and Pope Pius VII reorganized the Church in France after the Revolution and the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Signed on July 15, 1801, ratified by Pius VII on August 15 and by Napoleon on September 8, it reduced the number of French dioceses to about sixty, required the resignation of the bishops in office — a measure that forty-five of the ninety-seven "refractory" bishops of the Ancien Régime refused, giving rise to the small schismatic Church — and reorganized the hierarchy under criteria of conciliation. Pius VII later protested against the "Organic Articles," added by Napoleon without his knowledge.

In the twentieth century, the Lateran Treaty, signed on February 11, 1929 between Pius XI and Mussolini, created the Vatican City State, recognized Catholicism as the religion of the Italian State, and compensated the Church for the loss of the Papal States, ending the Roman Question. In Brazil, relations between the State and the Holy See were consolidated by the Agreement concerning the Juridical Status of the Catholic Church in Brazil, signed in Vatican City on November 13, 2008 by Celso Amorim, Minister of Foreign Affairs, and Archbishop Dominique Mamberti, Secretary for Relations with States. Composed of a preamble and twenty articles, it dealt with the juridical status of the Church, the recognition of academic degrees, religious education in public schools, canonical marriage, and the tax regime. It was approved by the National Congress through Legislative Decree no. 698, of October 7, 2009, entered into force internationally on December 10, 2009, and was promulgated by Decree no. 7,107, of February 11, 2010. Its passage through the legislative process raised criticism regarding its compatibility with the secular nature of the State and the equitable treatment of other religious denominations.

itens.resumo: A canonical censure that forbids participation in certain liturgical acts and sacraments, without excluding the person from the communion of the Church as excommunication does; historically also applied to entire territories.
itens.corpo:
The interdict is an ecclesiastical censure less grave than excommunication: it deprives the faithful of participating in certain acts of worship — receiving some sacraments, exercising liturgical functions, administering sacramentals — but, unlike excommunication, it does not exclude the person from the communion of the Church or from all of their rights. The 1983 Code of Canon Law defines it by reference: the interdict subjects the person to the prohibitions listed in can. 1331 § 1, nn. 1 and 2 (can. 1332), that is, to the same liturgical prohibitions as excommunication, but without the effects on governance that the latter entails. It further provides (can. 1331 § 2) that, when imposed or declared, others must prevent the person under interdict from acting in ministerial functions in the liturgy, and the censured person may not be admitted to Communion (cf. can. 915).

Historically the interdict could be personal, applied to specific individuals, or local — laid upon a city, a kingdom or an entire region, suspending almost all sacramental and liturgical life. This collective form carried enormous weight at the height of medieval Christendom. The most famous case is the interdict laid by Pope Innocent III upon England and Wales: faced with King John Lackland's refusal to accept Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury, the pontiff ordered the English bishops to publish the interdict on March 23, 1208. Churches were closed, the sacraments were forbidden — except baptism, confession and viaticum for the dying — and burial in consecrated ground was prohibited. The king was excommunicated in 1209; he was only reconciled with the Church in 1213, and the interdict was only finally lifted in July 1214, after more than six years.

With the Second Vatican Council and the revision of penal discipline, the general or local interdict fell into disuse. The motu proprio De Episcoporum Muneribus of Paul VI (June 15, 1966), in implementation of the conciliar doctrine on the authority of bishops, removed from bishops the faculty to decree the collective interdict, restricting the measure to rare and reserved cases. In the 1983 Code the interdict subsists chiefly as a personal censure — latae sententiae or ferendae sententiae — retaining its medicinal character: it seeks to lead the faithful to conversion, the censure being remissible once contumacy has ceased. Among the typical cases in which it may be applied on its own are offenses such as those provided for in canons 1370 to 1374 (cf. can. 1373, which punishes with interdict or other just penalties anyone who publicly stirs up animosity or hatred against the Apostolic See or the Ordinary).

itens.resumo: An ancient privilege, now extinct, by which the Holy See granted kings and rulers the right to present candidates for bishoprics and ecclesiastical benefices in their territories, with the final decision remaining with the Church.
itens.corpo:
The padroado (from the Latin jus patronatus) was the set of privileges that the Holy See granted to monarchs who founded or supported churches and missions, including the right to present (nominate) suitable persons to fill bishoprics and other ecclesiastical benefices, while the final canonical provision belonged to the ecclesiastical authority. The system arose in the context of the Iberian overseas conquests and the bulls dividing the New World. In 1493, Pope Alexander VI issued the bulls Inter caetera (May 4), which granted to the Catholic Monarchs the lands west of a meridian drawn one hundred leagues from the Azores and Cape Verde islands, on the grounds of the propagation of the faith — a line later shifted by the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494).

In Portugal, the padroado was consolidated by a series of bulls of Leo X. By Dum fidei constantiam, of June 7, 1514, the Pope granted to the King of Portugal and the Algarve and to his successors "the right of patronage and of presenting suitable persons for any churches and ecclesiastical benefices" in the territories conquered or to be conquered from the infidels, with the churches being united to the Order of Christ. Other bulls of the same year, such as Cum sicut magestas and Pro excellenti praeeminentia (June 14, which created the Diocese of Funchal), expanded these powers. In practice, the Portuguese Crown acquired broad influence over the appointment of bishops and ecclesiastical administration in Africa, Asia and Brazil.

In Brazil, the Portuguese Padroado — inherited by the Empire after independence — was combined with the royal placet (the imperial "passe" by which papal documents and norms were in force in the country only after approval by the emperor). This subjection of the Church to the State was at the heart of the so-called Religious Question (c. 1872-1875). On March 3, 1872, the Bishop of Olinda, Dom Vital Maria Gonçalves de Oliveira, and the Bishop of Pará, Dom Antônio de Macedo Costa, both ultramontane, placed under interdict confraternities that sheltered members of Freemasonry, basing themselves on papal directives (such as the Syllabus of Errors of 1864 by Pius IX) that had not been approved by the Empire. Refusing to revoke the interdicts, they were denounced for civil disobedience. On February 21, 1874, the Supreme Court of Justice sentenced Dom Vital to four years in prison with forced labor, a penalty later commuted to simple imprisonment by Emperor Pedro II; the bishop was held at the Fortress of São João, in Rio de Janeiro. Dom Macedo Costa received a similar sentence. Both enjoyed great influence: according to the 1872 Census, 99.7% of Brazilians were Catholic.

The diplomatic pressure of the Holy See, the fall of the cabinet of the Baron of Rio Branco, and the demand of the Duke of Caxias as a condition for taking over the government led Pedro II to yield. By decree of September 17, 1875, the two bishops were granted amnesty and returned in triumph to their dioceses. On April 29, 1876, Pius IX addressed to them the encyclical Exortae in ista, warning that the lifting of the interdicts did not mean tolerance of Freemasonry. The padroado regime in Brazil was only abolished with the separation of Church and State, formalized in the republican Constitution of 1891 (art. 72). The institution of jus patronatus, still regulated in canons 1448 ff. of the 1917 Code of Canon Law, was not retained in the 1983 Code.

itens.resumo: The loss of the rights and duties proper to a cleric, granted by a rescript of the Holy See or imposed as a penalty, without erasing the sacramental character of ordination.
itens.corpo:
Reduction to the lay state — called "loss of the clerical state" in the previous Code — is the act by which a cleric ceases to enjoy the rights and to be subject to the obligations proper to his state, is forbidden to exercise the power of orders, and is deprived of all the ecclesiastical offices and responsibilities he held. It may occur by way of grace, through a rescript of the Apostolic See granted at the request of the cleric himself, or by way of penalty, as a penalty imposed at the end of a judicial process for a most grave delict, such as the sexual abuse of minors.

Canon Law is clear in distinguishing this juridical effect from the sacramental effect of ordination: the character imprinted by the sacrament of Holy Orders is considered indelible, so that a cleric reduced to the lay state remains, theologically, a priest, even though he can no longer publicly exercise that ministry. The measure is not irreversible: in exceptional circumstances, the competent authority may restore to the clerical state one who was reduced from it.
fontes: Code of Canon Law, canons 290-293
Sacred Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Norms on the procedure for reduction to the lay state (January 13, 1971)

itens.titulo: Sanation in the Root (Sanatio in Radice)
itens.resumo: A canonical instrument that convalidates, without renewal of consent, a marriage that was null from its beginning, with its effects retroacting to the moment of the celebration.
itens.corpo:
Sanation in the root is an institute by which the competent ecclesiastical authority — the Holy See or, in many cases, the diocesan bishop — convalidates a marriage celebrated invalidly, without requiring the parties to renew their matrimonial consent, as is normally required in simple convalidation. The act dispenses, when present, the impediment that rendered the bond null, and also the canonical form if it was not observed, with the juridical and canonical effects of the marriage retroacting to the moment at which it was originally celebrated.

It is a remedy intended above all for situations in which the renewal of consent would be impossible or extremely inconvenient — for example, when one of the parties no longer knows of the original defect. For this reason, the Code requires that it be probable that the spouses wish to persevere in conjugal life, and it cannot be granted when the matrimonial consent itself is lacking in one of the parties at the moment the sanation is requested.
fontes: Code of Canon Law, canons 1161-1165

itens.resumo: An institution, based on the teaching of Saint Paul in Scripture, that allows the dissolution of a valid but non-sacramental marriage between two unbaptized persons when one of them converts and the other does not agree to remain peacefully in the union.
itens.corpo:
The Pauline privilege, grounded in the First Letter of Paul to the Corinthians (7:12-15), allows the dissolution — not merely a declaration of nullity — of a legitimate and valid marriage that is not sacramental, contracted between two unbaptized persons, when one of them receives baptism and the other refuses to live peacefully with that person or to do so without offense to the Creator. In this case, the marriage is dissolved "in favor of the faith" of the converted party at the moment that party contracts a new marriage.

It is clearly distinguished from matrimonial nullity: it is not declared that the bond never existed, but that a real and valid bond can be broken by the privilege of the faith, when conversion to Christianity is put at risk by continuing in the previous union. The institution does not apply if either party was already a baptized Christian at the time of the celebration of the original marriage.
fontes: Code of Canon Law, canons 1143-1147
1 Corinthians 7:12-15

itens.resumo: A legislative document that the pope issues "on his own initiative," without depending on a prior proposal from a dicastery of the Roman Curia.
itens.corpo:
"Motu proprio" is a Latin expression meaning "on one's own initiative": it designates a pontifical document personally signed by the pope, on his own decision, and not in response to a petition or proposal from others. It is one of the instruments by which the Roman Pontiff can legislate, create or reform institutions of the Roman Curia, amend norms of the Code of Canon Law, or address specific disciplinary matters.

Although historically associated with matters of lesser doctrinal weight, the motu proprio has been used for decisions of great institutional reach — from the creation of new dicasteries to procedural reforms of the Code itself, such as the simplification of matrimonial nullity processes promoted by Francis in 2015. The first papal motu proprio on record was promulgated by Innocent VIII in 1484.
fontes: Francis, Apostolic Letter in the form of a Motu Proprio «Humanam Progressionem» (2016)
Catholic Encyclopedia, entry "Motu Proprio"

itens.resumo: Motu proprio of Pope Francis that established, for the whole Church, mandatory procedures for reporting and investigating sexual abuse and its cover-up by bishops and religious superiors.
itens.corpo:
Signed by Pope Francis on May 7, 2019, and in force since June 1 of that year, "Vos Estis Lux Mundi" introduced, for the first time in the whole Catholic Church, the obligation for clerics and religious to report cases of sexual abuse of which they are aware, and also required each diocese to set up a system, easily accessible to the public, for receiving reports. The document also created a specific procedure for investigating bishops and major religious superiors accused of having committed abuse or of having covered up the conduct of others.

When the report involves a bishop, it must be sent to the Holy See or to the metropolitan of the respective ecclesiastical province, who conducts a preliminary investigation under Roman supervision. The text was updated and made definitive by a new motu proprio of March 25, 2023, which repealed the 2019 version and extended, among other points, the obligation to cooperate with investigating authorities to lay people holding positions of ecclesial leadership as well.
fontes: Francis, Apostolic Letter in the form of a Motu Proprio "Vos Estis Lux Mundi" (May 7, 2019)
Francis, "Vos Estis Lux Mundi" - updated text (March 25, 2023)

itens.titulo: The Lifting of the Pontifical Secret in Abuse Cases (2019)
itens.resumo: Decision of Pope Francis to remove the classification of "pontifical secret" from reports and proceedings concerning the sexual abuse of minors, distinct from the sacramental seal of confession.
itens.corpo:
On December 6, 2019, Pope Francis determined, by rescript, that canonical administrative and penal proceedings concerning offenses of sexual violence and abuse of minors committed by clerics would no longer be covered by the "pontifical secret" — the highest degree of documentary confidentiality in the Roman Curia. The measure requires dioceses and dicasteries to provide reports, testimonies and procedural documents to the competent civil authorities whenever requested by law.

The decision does not alter in any way the sacramental seal of confession, which is of an absolutely distinct nature and inviolable even in these cases. The stated purpose of the change was to remove an obstacle that, according to the Holy See itself, had been invoked to deny information to victims, families and civil authorities, in contradiction with the commitment to greater transparency undertaken by the Church after the sexual abuse crisis.
fontes: Francis, Rescriptum ex Audientia SS.mi on the confidentiality of proceedings (December 6, 2019)
Vatican News, "The Pope abolished the pontifical secret for cases of sexual abuse" (December 17, 2019)

itens.titulo: Canon 915: The Discipline of Admission to Holy Communion
itens.resumo: Canonical norm that excludes from Eucharistic Communion those who are excommunicated, those under interdict, and those who obstinately persist in manifest grave sin.
itens.corpo:
Canon 915 of the Code of Canon Law establishes that those who have been excommunicated or interdicted after the imposition or declaration of the penalty, and others who obstinately persist in manifest grave sin, are not to be admitted to holy Communion. The Church understands this restriction not as an arbitrary punishment, but as a recognition that, for as long as such a situation lasts, the faithful person has placed himself outside the full Eucharistic communion that the sacrament presupposes — a reading supported by Saint Paul's warning against receiving the Eucharist unworthily (1 Cor 11:27-29).

The practical application of the norm is frequently debated, especially when it involves public figures in situations of notorious disagreement with fundamental moral teachings of the Church. The Code entrusts the discernment of each concrete case to the minister who presides at the celebration, within criteria of pastoral prudence and the guidelines of the local bishops.
fontes: Code of Canon Law, canon 915
1 Corinthians 11:27-29

itens.resumo: A category of particularly grave canonical crimes — such as the sexual abuse of minors by clerics — whose judgment is reserved to the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith.
itens.corpo:
"Delicta graviora" ("more grave offenses") is the technical designation for a set of canonical crimes considered especially grave against the faith, the sacraments, or morals, whose prosecution Church law reserves to the Dicastery (formerly Congregation) for the Doctrine of the Faith, rather than to the ordinary diocesan tribunals. The list includes offenses against the sanctity of the Eucharist and of sacramental confession — such as the violation of the sacramental seal — and, since the reform promoted by John Paul II in 2001, the sexual abuse of minors committed by clerics.

The norms that regulate these offenses, entitled "Sacramentorum Sanctitatis Tutela," were reinforced by Benedict XVI in 2010, extending prescription periods and also defining as an offense the possession and distribution of child pornography by clerics, and were updated once again by Francis in 2021, to harmonize them with that year's reform of Book VI of the Code of Canon Law.
fontes: John Paul II, Motu Proprio «Sacramentorum Sanctitatis Tutela» (2001)
Francis, Updated Norms on the Delicts Reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (2021)

itens.resumo: The period after which an ecclesiastical criminal action is extinguished, longer for the most serious offenses reserved to the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith.
itens.corpo:
Canon Law provides, like civil legislation, for limitation periods for ecclesiastical criminal action: according to canon 1362, the general rule is three years counted from the day on which the offense was committed (or, if it is permanent or habitual, from the day on which it ceased), unless particular law provides otherwise. For offenses reserved to the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith — among them the sexual abuse of minors by clerics — and for some other especially grave offenses provided for in the Code itself, the period is seven years, having been successively extended in recent decades.

The reform of Book VI of the Code, promoted by Pope Francis and in force since December 2021, made the determination of penalties more precise and strengthened procedural guarantees, including the very regime of prescription, in a declared effort to make the Church's penal justice more effective and clearer.
fontes: Code of Canon Law, canon 1362

itens.resumo: The periodic obligation of diocesan bishops to venerate the tombs of Peter and Paul in Rome and to present themselves to the Pope with a report on the state of their diocese.
itens.corpo:
The Latin expression "ad limina Apostolorum" means "to the thresholds of the Apostles," referring to the Roman basilicas of Saint Peter and Saint Paul Outside the Walls. The Code of Canon Law (canons 399-400) obliges each diocesan bishop to visit the tombs of the two apostles periodically — in practice, every five years —, to present himself in person to the Roman Pontiff, and to submit a detailed report on the pastoral, administrative, and spiritual situation of his diocese.

In current practice, the visit also includes meetings of the bishops of each region or country with the various dicasteries of the Roman Curia, serving as a concrete instrument of what the ecclesiology of Vatican II calls collegial communion between the bishops and the successor of Peter — a periodic gesture of visible unity between the particular Churches and the See of Rome.
fontes: Code of Canon Law, canons 399-400
